overview.text: Glucose is a simple sugar (a monosaccharide) with six carbon atoms and the formula C6H12O6. It is important because cells break it down during cellular respiration to make ATP, a usable form of energy. Plants make glucose and may join extra molecules into starch for storage; animals store glucose mainly as glycogen, while plants also use glucose units to build cellulose, a strong part of cell walls. In people, glucose carried in blood is called blood sugar: when its level rises, the pancreas releases insulin, which helps glucose enter cells. In water, glucose is usually in a ring-shaped form.

key_facts.text: Glucose is a six-carbon sugar, or hexose, and its chemical formula is C6H12O6.
Glucose is a monosaccharide—the single-unit sugar that can serve as a building block for larger carbohydrates.
Cells use energy released from glucose in cellular respiration to help make ATP.
Starch and glycogen store glucose; cellulose is made of glucose units and helps strengthen plant cell walls.
When blood glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, which helps glucose move into cells for energy.
